arXiv:2104.05339v1 [math.AG] 12 Apr 2021

Endomorphisms of quasi-projective varieties - towards Zariski dense orbit and Kawaguchi-Silverman conjectures

Jia Jia, Takahiro Shibata, Junyi Xie, and De-Qi Zhang Address: National University of Singapore, Singapore 119076, Republic of Singapore Email address: jia_jia@nus.edu.sg Address: National University of Singapore, Singapore 119076, Republic of Singapore Email address: mattash@nus.edu.sg Address: Univ Rennes, CNRS, IRMAR - UMR 6625, F-35000 Rennes, France Email address: junyi.xie@univ-rennes1.fr Address: National University of Singapore, Singapore 119076, Republic of Singapore Email address: matzdq@nus.edu.sg
Abstract.

Let XX be a quasi-projective variety and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a finite surjective endomorphism. We consider Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture (ZDO), and Adelic Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture (AZO). We consider also Kawaguchi-Silverman Conjecture (KSC) asserting that the (first) dynamical degree d1​(f)d_{1}(f) of ff equals the arithmetic degree αf​(P)\alpha_{f}(P) at a point PP having Zariski dense ff-forward orbit. Assuming XX is a smooth affine surface, such that the log Kodaira dimension κ¯​(X)\overline{\kappa}(X) is non-negative (resp. the étale fundamental group π1ét​(X)\pi_{1}^{\text{\'{e}t}}(X) is infinite), we confirm AZO, (hence) ZDO, and KSC (when deg⁡(f)≥2\operatorname{deg}(f)\geq 2) (resp. AZO and hence ZDO). We also prove ZDO (resp. AZO and hence ZDO) for every surjective endomorphism on any projective variety with “larger” first dynamical degree (resp. every dominant endomorphism of any semiabelian variety).

Key words and phrases: 
Endomorphism, Dynamical degree, Arithmetical degree, Semiabelian variety, Affine surface, Log Kodaira dimension

1. Introduction

We work over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 00 unless otherwise stated.

The motivation of the paper is the following Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture (ZDO), Adelic Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture (AZO) and Kawaguchi-Silverman Conjecture (KSC).

Conjecture 1.1 (Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture=ZDO).

Let XX be a variety over k and f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X a dominant rational map. If the f∗f^{*}-invariant function field k​(X)f=k\textbf{k}(X)^{f}=\textbf{k}, then there exists some x∈X⁡(k)x\in X(\textbf{k}) whose ff-orbit Of​(x)≔{fn​(x)∣n≥0}O_{f}(x)\coloneqq\{f^{n}(x)\mid n\geq 0\} is well-defined, i.e., ff is defined at fn​(x)f^{n}(x) for any n≥0n\geq 0, and Zariski dense in XX.

When the transcendence degree of k over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is finite, in [Xie19, Section 3], the third author has introduced the adelic topology on X⁡(k)X(\textbf{k}) and proposed the Adelic Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture (AZO):

Conjecture 1.2 (Adelic Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture=AZO).

Assume the hypothesis that the transcendence degree of k over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is finite. Let XX be a variety over k and f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X a dominant rational map. If the f∗f^{*}-invariant function field k​(X)f=k\textbf{k}(X)^{f}=\textbf{k}, then there exists a nonempty adelic open subset A⊆X⁡(k)A\subseteq X(\textbf{k}) such that for every point x∈Ax\in A the ff-orbit Of​(x)O_{f}(x) is well-defined and Zariski dense in XX.

Conjecture 1.3 (Kawaguchi-Silverman Conjecture=KSC; cf. [KS16]).

Let XX be a quasi-projective variety over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X a dominant rational map. Take a point x∈X⁡(ℚ¯)x\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}). If the ff-orbit Of​(x)O_{f}(x) is well-defined and Zariski dense in XX, then the limit αf​(x)\alpha_{f}(x) (called the arithmetic degree) as defined in 3.9, converges and equals d1​(f)d_{1}(f), the first dynamical degree of ff (cf. 3.1).

Remark 1.4.

AZO 1.2 implies ZDO 1.1. Indeed, even the hypothesis on k in AZO 1.2 does not cause any problem. To be precise, for every pair (X,f)(X,f) over any algebraically closed field k of characteristic zero, there exists an algebraically closed subfield KK of k whose transcendence degree over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is finite and such that (X,f)(X,f) is defined over KK, i.e., there exists a pair (XK,fK)(X_{K},f_{K}) such that (X,f)(X,f) is its base change by k. By [Xie19, Corollary 3.29], if AZO 1.2 holds for (XK,fK)(X_{K},f_{K}), then ZDO 1.1 holds for (X,f)(X,f).

In this paper, when we discuss AZO 1.2, we always assume that the transcendence degree of k over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is finite; when we discuss KSC 1.3, we always assume that k=ℚ¯\textbf{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}.

Theorems 1.5, 1.7, 1.8, 1.9, 1.11 and 1.12 are our main results.

We first deal with endomorphisms of semiabelian varieties: in Theorem 1.5 below, we prove AZO 1.2 and hence ZDO 1.1, while KSC 1.3 is known.

Theorem 1.5.

Assume that the transcendence degree of k over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is finite. Let GG be a semiabelian variety over k (cf. 2.1). Let f:G→Gf\colon G\to G be a dominant endomorphism. Then AZO 1.2 and hence ZDO 1.1 hold for (G,f)(G,f).

Remark 1.6.
  1. (1)

    Theorem 1.5 generalises [Xie19, Theorem 1.14] and [GS19, Theorem 1.1] from abelian varieties to semiabelian varieties.

  2. (2)

    AZO 1.2 and hence ZDO 1.1 are known for surjective endomorphisms of projective surfaces (cf. [Xie19], [JXZ20]).

  3. (3)

    KSC 1.3 is known for surjective endomorphisms of projective surfaces (cf. [MSS18], [MZ19]) and for surjective endomorphisms of semiabelian varieties (cf. [MS20]).

The next aim of this paper is to extend both AZO 1.2 and KSC 1.3 to affine surfaces. Recall the log Kodaira dimension κ¯⁡(X)\operatorname{\overline{\kappa}}(X) of a variety XX takes value in {−∞,0,…,dimX}\{-\infty,0,\dots,\dim X\} (cf. [Iit82, §11]). Theorem 1.7 below gives the structures of endomorphisms of smooth affine surfaces; note that when κ¯⁡(X)=2\operatorname{\overline{\kappa}}(X)=2, our ff is an automorphism of finite order (cf. Lemma 2.11). For the proof of Theorem 1.7, the main steps are given in [GZ08]. We simplify or supplement more details in the present paper.

Theorem 1.7.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a finite surjective morphism of degree ≥2\geq 2. Then we have:

  1. (1)

    Suppose κ¯⁡(X)=0\operatorname{\overline{\kappa}}(X)=0. Then XX is a Q-algebraic torus (cf. 2.1). Precisely, there is a finite étale cover τ:T→X\tau\colon T\to X from an algebraic torus T≅𝔾m2T\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}; further, τ\tau can be chosen such that ff lifts to a surjective morphism fT:T→Tf_{T}\colon T\to T.

  2. (2)

    Suppose κ¯⁡(X)=1\operatorname{\overline{\kappa}}(X)=1. Then there is a finite étale cover X′′→XX^{\prime\prime}\to X such that X′′=𝔾m×B′′X^{\prime\prime}=\mathbb{G}_{m}\times B^{\prime\prime} where B′′B^{\prime\prime} is a smooth affine curve with κ¯⁡(B′′)=1\operatorname{\overline{\kappa}}(B^{\prime\prime})=1, and ff (after iteration) lifts to an endomorphism f′′f^{\prime\prime} on X′′X^{\prime\prime} such that π′′∘f′′=π′′\pi^{\prime\prime}\circ f^{\prime\prime}=\pi^{\prime\prime}, where the natural projection π′′:X′′→B′′\pi^{\prime\prime}\colon X^{\prime\prime}\to B^{\prime\prime} is the lifting of an Iitaka fibration of XX.

As a consequence of the above structural theorem, we confirm both AZO 1.2 and KSC 1.3 for smooth affine surfaces of non-negative log Kodaira dimension.

Theorem 1.8.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a finite surjective endomorphism. Suppose κ¯⁡(X)≥0\operatorname{\overline{\kappa}}(X)\geq 0. Then:

  1. (1)

    AZO 1.2 and hence ZDO 1.1 hold for (X,f)(X,f).

  2. (2)

    If k=ℚ¯\textbf{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}} and deg⁡(f)≥2\deg(f)\geq 2, then KSC 1.3 holds for (X,f)(X,f).

We may replace the assumption on the log Kodaira dimension in Theorem 1.8 by the assumption on the fundamental group of XX. Precisely, we have:

Theorem 1.9.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a finite surjective endomorphism. Suppose the étale fundamental group π1e´​t​(X)\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X) is infinite. Then we have:

  1. (1)

    AZO 1.2 and hence ZDO 1.1 hold for (X,f)(X,f).

  2. (2)

    Suppose k=ℚ¯\textbf{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, deg⁡(f)≥2\deg(f)\geq 2 and X≇𝔸1×𝔾mX\not\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}. Then KSC 1.3 holds for (X,f)(X,f).

  3. (3)

    Suppose that κ¯​(X)=−∞\overline{\kappa}(X)=-\infty. Then ff descends along an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration of XX, hence KSC 1.3 holds for (X,f)(X,f) when deg⁡(f)=1\deg(f)=1 and k=ℚ¯\textbf{k}=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}.

Remark 1.10.

On Theorem 1.9, we have:

  1. (1)

    In the proof of Theorem 1.9, we actually prove a stronger statement as follows (cf. Lemma 2.16). Assume that the transcendence degree of k over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is finite. Fix an embedding τ:k↪ℂ\tau\colon\textbf{k}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C} and denote by XℂX_{\mathbb{C}} the base change of XX by ℂ\mathbb{C} via τ\tau. If the fundamental group π1​(Xℂ)\pi_{1}(X_{\mathbb{C}}) is infinite, then AZO 1.2 holds for (X,f)(X,f).

  2. (2)

    The case where π1e´​t​(X)\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X) is finite seems harder, but we remark that ZDO 1.1 holds for surjective endomorphisms of 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}, where π1e´​t​(𝔸2)=(1)\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(\mathbb{A}^{2})=(1) (cf. [Xie17]).

  3. (3)

    At the moment, we are not able to prove KSC 1.3 when X≅𝔸1×𝔾mX\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}.

We return to higher-dimensional ZDO 1.1 and KSC 1.3. In Section 3, we first prove some basic properties of the arithmetic degree for dominant rational self-maps f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X on singular varieties XX. In particular, Proposition 3.11 generalises the upper bound of the arithmetic degree by the dynamical degree from smooth varieties to singular varieties (cf. [Mat20, Theorem 1.4], also [KS16] when ff is a morphism and XX is smooth projective).

In Theorem 1.11 below, we prove AZO 1.2 for a class of upper triangular rational self-maps. It generalises the result in [MS14, Theorem 7.16] for ZDO 1.1 for split polynomial endomorphisms. A surjective endomorphism of X=𝔸1×𝔾mX=\mathbb{A}^{1}\times\mathbb{G}_{m} is a special case of it (cf. Theorem 7.3) and is used in the proof of Theorem 1.9.

Theorem 1.11.

Let f:𝔸m⇢𝔸mf\colon\mathbb{A}^{m}\dashrightarrow\mathbb{A}^{m} be a dominant rational self-map taking the form

(x1,…,xm)↦(f1​(x1),f2​(x1,x2),…,fm​(x1,…,xm))(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})\mapsto(f_{1}(x_{1}),f_{2}(x_{1},x_{2}),\dots,f_{m}(x_{1},\dots,x_{m}))

where f1∈k(x1),f2∈k(x1)[x2],…,fm∈k(x1,…,xm−1)[xm]f_{1}\in\textbf{k}(x_{1}),f_{2}\in\textbf{k}(x_{1})[x_{2}],\dots,f_{m}\in\textbf{k}(x_{1},\dots,x_{m-1})[x_{m}].

Then AZO 1.2 and hence ZDO 1.1 hold for (𝔸m,f)(\mathbb{A}^{m},f).

In the last part of the paper, we introduce a method to study ZDO 1.1 via arithmetic degree. Using this method, we obtain some sufficient conditions for ZDO 1.1 for endomorphisms of higher dimensional projective varieties. Below is a sample result saying that ZDO 1.1 holds true for those ff with larger first dynamical degree d1​(f)d_{1}(f).

Theorem 1.12.

Let f:X→Xf\colon X\to X be a dominant endomorphism of a projective variety over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}. Then ZDO 1.1 holds if one of the following conditions is satisfied.

  1. (1)

    dimX=2\dim X=2, d1​(f)>1d_{1}(f)>1 and d1​(f)≥d2​(f)d_{1}(f)\geq d_{2}(f); or

  2. (2)

    dimX=3\dim X=3, and d1​(f)>d3​(f)=1d_{1}(f)>d_{3}(f)=1; or

  3. (3)

    XX is smooth of dimension d≥2d\geq 2, and d1​(f)>maxi=2d​{di​(f)}d_{1}(f)>\max_{i=2}^{d}\{d_{i}(f)\}.

2. General preliminary results

2.1.

Notation and Terminology

By a variety we mean an algebraic variety, i.e., an integral separated scheme of finite type over the field k. On a smooth variety VV, a reduced divisor DD is of simple normal crossing (SNC for short) if every irreducible component of DD is smooth and locally D={x1⋯xs=0}D=\{x_{1}\cdots x_{s}=0\} at every point of DD with local coordinates x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n} of VV.

Let XX be a smooth quasi-projective variety. A pair (V,D)(V,D) is called a compactification of XX if VV is a projective variety containing XX as an open subset and D=V∖XD=V\setminus X. A compactification (V,D)(V,D) of XX is a log smooth compatification if VV is smooth and DD is an SNC divisor.

Given a log smooth compactification (V,D)(V,D) of XX, the log Kodaira dimension κ¯​(X)\overline{\kappa}(X) is defined as the following Iitaka dimension

κ¯​(X)=κ⁡(V,KV+D),\overline{\kappa}(X)=\kappa(V,K_{V}+D),

which takes value in {−∞,0,1,…,dimX}\{-\infty,0,1,\dots,\dim X\}. The characteristic property of κ=κ¯⁡(X)\kappa=\operatorname{\overline{\kappa}}(X) is:

α​sκ≤dimH0​(V,s⁡(KV+D))≤β​sκ\alpha s^{\kappa}\leq\dim H^{0}(V,s(K_{V}+D))\leq\beta s^{\kappa}

for some constants 0<α<β0<\alpha<\beta and sufficiently large and divisible ss. The definition of κ¯​(X)\overline{\kappa}(X) is independent of the choice of the log smooth compactification. For details, see [Iit82, §11].

We use 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} to denote the 11-dimensional algebraic torus, 𝔾mn\mathbb{G}_{m}^{n} the nn-dimensional algebraic torus, and 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} the 11-dimensional additive algebraic group. By a semiabelian variety XX, we mean the extension

1⟶T⟶X⟶A⟶01\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow X\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow 0

of an abelian variety AA by an algebraic torus TT. A variety XX is called a Q-algebraic torus if there is a finite étale cover T→XT\to X from an algebraic torus TT.

Let XX be a variety over k and f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X a rational map. For any field extension k⊆L\textbf{k}\subseteq L, denote by (XL,fL)(X_{L},f_{L}) the base change of (X,f)(X,f) by LL.

Lemma 2.2.

Let XX be a smooth affine variety of dimension d≥2d\geq 2. Then we have:

  1. (1)

    Let (V,D)(V,D) be any compactification of XX. Then DD is the support of a connected big effective divisor. Moreover, when d=2d=2, DD is the support of a connected ample effective divisor.

  2. (2)

    There is a log smooth compactification (V,D)(V,D) of XX such that DD is the support of a connected nef and big effective divisor.

Proof.

Let (V,D)(V,D) be any compactification of XX. By [Har70, Ch. II, §3], DD has pure codimension 11 and is connected. Embedding XX to an affine space 𝔸n\mathbb{A}^{n} and taking its (normalised) closure in ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n}, we can take a compactification (V0,D0)(V_{0},D_{0}) of XX such that D0D_{0} is the support of an ample effective divisor D0′D_{0}^{\prime} of a normal projective variety V0V_{0}. Taking a log resolution of (V0,D0)(V_{0},D_{0}), we obtain a log smooth compactification (V′,D′)(V^{\prime},D^{\prime}) of XX such that D′D^{\prime} is the support of a connected effective nef and big divisor (the pullback of D0′D_{0}^{\prime}), which proves (2). Let (V′′,D′′)(V^{\prime\prime},D^{\prime\prime}) be another log smooth compactification of XX dominating both (V′,D′)(V^{\prime},D^{\prime}) and (V,D)(V,D). Then D′′D^{\prime\prime} is the inverse image of D0D_{0} and hence the support of a connected effective big divisor, and DD is the image of D′′D^{\prime\prime} and hence also the support of a connected effective big divisor. For the case dimX=2\dim X=2, see [Har70, Ch. II, §4]. ∎

Lemma 2.3.

Let VV be a smooth projective surface with a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration π:V→B\pi\colon V\to B to a smooth projective curve BB. Let FF be any fibre of π\pi. If FF contains just one (−1)(-1)-curve, then its coefficient in FF is at least 22.

Proof.

This follows by induction on the number of irreducible components of FF. ∎

Definition 2.4.

Let XX be a smooth quasi-projective surface and π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle over a smooth curve BB. We say that π\pi is untwisted if some (and hence every) compactification π¯:X¯→B¯\overline{\pi}\colon\overline{X}\to\overline{B} of π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B has exactly two cross-sections as the horizontal part of the boundary X¯∖X\overline{X}\setminus X.

Lemma 2.5.

Let XX be a smooth quasi-projective surface and π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle over a smooth curve BB. Then we can take log smooth compactifications X⊆X¯X\subseteq\overline{X}, B⊆B¯B\subseteq\overline{B} such that π\pi extends to a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-bundle π¯:X¯→B¯\overline{\pi}\colon\overline{X}\to\overline{B}. Moreover, if π\pi is untwisted, then we can take them such that X¯∖X\overline{X}\setminus X consists of exactly two disjoint cross-sections and some fibres.

Proof.

Take log smooth compactifications X⊆X¯X\subseteq\overline{X}, B⊆B¯B\subseteq\overline{B} such that π\pi extends to π¯:X¯→B¯\overline{\pi}\colon\overline{X}\to\overline{B}. Take any point b∈B¯b\in\overline{B} and set F=π¯∗​bF=\overline{\pi}^{*}b. Suppose FF is reducible. If b∈B¯∖Bb\in\overline{B}\setminus B, then F⊆X¯∖XF\subseteq\overline{X}\setminus X, and we can contract (−1)(-1)-curves so that FF is irreducible. Assume b∈Bb\in B. Let F0≅ℙ1F_{0}\cong\mathbb{P}^{1} be the closure of π−1​(b)\pi^{-1}(b) in X¯\overline{X}. Now FF contains at least one (−1)(-1)-curve F1F_{1} since π¯\overline{\pi} is a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration. If F1F_{1} is the only (−1)(-1)-curve in FF, then its multiplicity in FF is at least 22 by Lemma 2.3. So F1≠F0F_{1}\neq F_{0} in this case. As a consequence, we have a (−1)(-1)-curve F1≠F0F_{1}\neq F_{0} in FF. We contract F1F_{1} (without touching XX) and continue this process; eventually we can make FF irreducible (and smooth). Thus we can assume π¯\overline{\pi} is a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-bundle.

Assume that π\pi is untwisted. Let H1,H2⊆X¯∖XH_{1},H_{2}\subseteq\overline{X}\setminus X be two cross-sections. If the intersection H1∩H2≠∅H_{1}\cap H_{2}\neq\varnothing, it lies in X¯∖X\overline{X}\setminus X since π−1​(b)=𝔾m\pi^{-1}(b)=\mathbb{G}_{m} for every b∈Bb\in B. So we can make H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} disjoint by blowing up and down repeatedly in X¯∖X\overline{X}\setminus X. ∎

Lemma 2.6.

Let XX be a smooth quasi-projective surface and π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle over a smooth curve BB. Then we have:

  1. (1)

    There is a finite étale cover B′→BB^{\prime}\to B of degree ≤2\leq 2 inducing a finite étale cover X′≔X×BB′→XX^{\prime}\coloneqq X\times_{B}B^{\prime}\to X and a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle X′→B′X^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} which is untwisted.

  2. (2)

    The log Kodaira dimensions satisfy κ¯​(X′)=κ¯​(X)=κ¯​(B)=κ¯​(B′)\overline{\kappa}(X^{\prime})=\overline{\kappa}(X)=\overline{\kappa}(B)=\overline{\kappa}(B^{\prime}).

  3. (3)

    Assume that π\pi is untwisted and BB is a smooth rational affine curve. Then π\pi is a trivial 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle.

Proof.

(1) Take log smooth compactifications X⊆X¯X\subseteq\overline{X}, B⊆B¯B\subseteq\overline{B} such that π\pi extends to π¯:X¯→B¯\overline{\pi}\colon\overline{X}\to\overline{B}. Let D=X¯∖X=H+ED=\overline{X}\setminus X=H+E where HH is the sum of horizontal components and EE is that of vertical components. If HH is irreducible, then H→B¯H\to\overline{B} restricts to a finite étale cover B′→BB^{\prime}\to B, since X→BX\to B is a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle. Let B′¯→H\overline{B^{\prime}}\to H be the normalisation, X′=X×BB′X^{\prime}=X\times_{B}B^{\prime} and X′¯\overline{X^{\prime}} the normalisation of X¯×B¯B′¯\overline{X}\times_{\overline{B}}\overline{B^{\prime}}. Then the projection X′→XX^{\prime}\to X is a finite étale cover, and the projection X′→B′X^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} which is still a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle will fit the next case. Indeed, the inverse of HH (⊆X¯\subseteq\overline{X}) in X′¯\overline{X^{\prime}} is a double section containing a cross-section, the compactification of {(b′,b′)∈X′∣b′∈B′}\{(b^{\prime},b^{\prime})\in X^{\prime}\mid b^{\prime}\in B^{\prime}\}, so it is the sum of two cross-sections.

(2) Since X′→XX^{\prime}\to X and B′→BB^{\prime}\to B are étale, we have κ¯​(X′)=κ¯​(X)\overline{\kappa}(X^{\prime})=\overline{\kappa}(X) and κ¯​(B′)=κ¯​(B)\overline{\kappa}(B^{\prime})=\overline{\kappa}(B) (cf. [Iit82, Theorem 11.10]). From now on, we assume that π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B is untwisted. Let H1,H2H_{1},H_{2} be cross-sections of π¯\overline{\pi} contained in DD. By Lemma 2.5, we may assume that π¯\overline{\pi} is a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-bundle and H1,H2H_{1},H_{2} are disjoint. Then we have KX¯+D∼π¯∗​(KB¯+L)K_{\overline{X}}+D\sim\overline{\pi}^{*}(K_{\overline{B}}+L) where L=B¯∖BL=\overline{B}\setminus B (cf. [Har77, Ch. V, Proposition 2.9, Lemma 2.10]). Thus κ¯​(X)=κ¯​(B)\overline{\kappa}(X)=\overline{\kappa}(B).

(3) Assume B=ℙ1∖(r​ points)B=\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus(r\text{ points}) with r≥1r\geq 1. Take log smooth compactifications X⊆X¯X\subseteq\overline{X}, B⊆B¯B\subseteq\overline{B}, as in Lemma 2.5, such that π\pi extends to a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-bundle π¯:X¯→B¯\overline{\pi}\colon\overline{X}\to\overline{B}, and the boundary D=X¯∖XD=\overline{X}\setminus X consists of exactly two disjoint cross-sections H1,H2H_{1},H_{2} and rr of fibres. By blowing up a point in a fibre over B¯∖B\overline{B}\setminus B and blowing down proper transform of the fibre and repeating the same process if necessary, we can make X¯≅ℙ1×ℙ1\overline{X}\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}\times\mathbb{P}^{1} without touching XX, and yet keep X¯∖X\overline{X}\setminus X being a union of two disjoint cross-sections and rr of fibres. Thus π\pi is a trivial 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle. ∎

Corollary 2.7.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface and π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle to a smooth curve BB. Then BB is affine.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.6, taking a finite étale base change, we may assume that π\pi is untwisted. By Lemma 2.5, we can embed π\pi to a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-bundle X¯→B¯\overline{X}\to\overline{B}, such that D≔X¯∖XD\coloneqq\overline{X}\setminus X is the sum of two disjoint cross-sections and the fibres over B¯∖B\overline{B}\setminus B. If B¯=B\overline{B}=B, then DD is not connected, a contradiction to Lemma 2.2. So BB is not projective. ∎

Definition 2.8.

Let π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B be a surjective morphism from a quasi-projective surface to a smooth curve. The multiplicity m=m⁡(F)m=m(F) of a fibre FF of π\pi is the greatest common divisor of coefficients in FF of all irreducible components of FF. We call FF a multiple fibre if m⁡(F)≥2m(F)\geq 2.

Proposition 2.9 (cf. [GMM20, Lemma 1.1.9]).

Let XX be a smooth quasi-projective surface and π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B a surjective morphism to a smooth curve BB. Let FjF_{j} (1≤j≤r)(1\leq j\leq r) be all multiple fibres of π\pi over bjb_{j}, with multiplicity mj≥2m_{j}\geq 2. Assume the hypothesis (⋆)(\star): either BB is affine, or BB is irrational, or r≥3r\geq 3, or r=2r=2 and m1=m2m_{1}=m_{2}. Then we have:

  1. (1)

    There is a finite morphism B′→BB^{\prime}\to B from a smooth curve, étale over B0≔B∖{b1,…,br}B_{0}\coloneqq B\setminus\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{r}\}, with ramification index mjm_{j} over bjb_{j}, and with X′X^{\prime} the normalisation of X×BB′X\times_{B}B^{\prime}, such that the projection X′→XX^{\prime}\to X is finite étale and the induced fibration X′→B′X^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} has no multiple fibre.

  2. (2)

    Assume further that every fibre of π\pi has support isomorphic to 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}. Then the fibration X′→B′X^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} is a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle over B′B^{\prime}.

Proof.

By the solution to Fenchel’s conjecture due to Fox, Bundgaard–Nielsen (cf. [BN51], [Cha83]), the hypothesis (⋆)(\star) implies the existence of a Galois covering B′→BB^{\prime}\to B, ramified precisely over bjb_{j} with index mjm_{j} for j=1,…,rj=1,\dots,r. Then the natural map X′→XX^{\prime}\to X from the normalisation X′X^{\prime} of X×BB′X\times_{B}B^{\prime} is étale by the smoothness of XX and the purity of branch loci. This proves (1), while (2) follows from (1) and the assumption that Fj=mj​[Fj]redF_{j}=m_{j}[F_{j}]_{\mathrm{red}}. ∎

It is now classical that on a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-factorial normal projective surface VV, every pseudo-effective ℚ\mathbb{Q}-divisor LL has the Zariski decomposition L=P+NL=P+N to the sum of two ℚ\mathbb{Q}-Cartier divisors such that:

  1. (1)

    PP is nef,

  2. (2)

    either N=0N=0 or NN is effective with Supp⁡N=⋃Ni\operatorname{Supp}N=\bigcup N_{i} the irreducible decomposition and with negative definite intersection matrix (Ni⋅Nj)(N_{i}\cdot N_{j}), and

  3. (3)

    (P⋅Ni)=0(P\cdot N_{i})=0 for every irreducible component NiN_{i} of Supp⁡N\operatorname{Supp}N.

We call PP (resp. NN) the nef part (resp. negative part) of the decomposition.

The following result is well known. We give a proof for the convenience of the reader.

Proposition 2.10.

Let VV be a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-factorial normal projective surface and DD an effective ℚ\mathbb{Q}-divisor such that (V,D)(V,D) has only log canonical singularities and L≔KV+DL\coloneqq K_{V}+D is pseudo-effective with L=P+NL=P+N its Zariski decomposition. Then PP is semi-ample and the inequality P≤LP\leq L induces isomorphisms H0​(V,𝒪⁡(s​P))≅H0​(V,𝒪⁡(s​L))H^{0}(V,\mathcal{O}(sP))\cong H^{0}(V,\mathcal{O}(sL)) for all ss sufficiently large and divisible.

Proof.

By the known Minimal Model Program for log canonical surfaces (cf. [Fuj12]), there is a composition

V=V0→π0V1→π1⋯→πm−1Vm≕WV=V_{0}\xrightarrow{\pi_{0}}V_{1}\xrightarrow{\pi_{1}}\cdots\xrightarrow{\pi_{m-1}}V_{m}\eqqcolon W

of birational contractions of (KVi+Di)(K_{V_{i}}+D_{i})-negative extremal curves Ei⊆ViE_{i}\subseteq V_{i} such that KW+DWK_{W}+D_{W} is nef and hence semi-ample by the abundance theorem (cf. [KM98, (3.13)]; here Di⊆ViD_{i}\subseteq V_{i} is the direct image of DD, and DW≔DmD_{W}\coloneqq D_{m}; further, KVi+Di=πi∗​(KVi+1+Di+1)+ai​EiK_{V_{i}}+D_{i}=\pi_{i}^{*}(K_{V_{i+1}}+D_{i+1})+a_{i}E_{i} for some ai>0a_{i}>0. Set π≔πm−1∘⋯∘π0:V→W\pi\coloneqq\pi_{m-1}\circ\cdots\circ\pi_{0}\colon V\to W. Then

L=KV+D=π∗​(KW+DW)+EL=K_{V}+D=\pi^{*}(K_{W}+D_{W})+E

where EE is effective and π\pi-exceptional. Thus P=π∗​(KW+D)P=\pi^{*}(K_{W}+D) and N=EN=E. The second isomorphism below follows from the projection formula:

H0​(V,𝒪​(s​L))\displaystyle H^{0}(V,\mathcal{O}(sL)) =H0​(W,π∗​𝒪​(s​L))≅H0​(W,𝒪⁡(s⁡(KW+DW))⊗π∗​𝒪​(s​E))\displaystyle=H^{0}(W,\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(sL))\cong H^{0}(W,\mathcal{O}(s(K_{W}+D_{W}))\otimes\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}(sE))
=H0​(W,𝒪⁡(s⁡(KW+DW))=H0​(V,𝒪⁡(s​P))CLOSE\displaystyle=H^{0}(W,\mathcal{O}(s(K_{W}+D_{W}))=H^{0}(V,\mathcal{O}(sP))

since E≥0E\geq 0 is π\pi-exceptional. ∎

Lemma 2.11 (cf. [Iit82, Theorem 11.6 and Theorem 11.12]).

Let XX be a variety and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a dominant morphism. Assume κ¯​(X)=dimX\overline{\kappa}(X)=\dim X. Then ff is an automorphism of finite order.

Lemma 2.12 (cf. [Iit77, Theorem 2]).

Let XX be a smooth variety with κ¯​(X)≥0\overline{\kappa}(X)\geq 0. Then any dominant morphism from XX into itself is an étale surjective morphism.

Lemma 2.13.

Let XX be a smooth variety and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a dominant morphism. Suppose that ff is étale and surjective (this is the case when κ¯​(X)≥0\overline{\kappa}(X)\geq 0; cf. Lemma 2.12). Suppose further that deg⁡(f)≥2\deg(f)\geq 2. Then the topological Euler number e⁡(X)e(X) of XX is 00.

Proof.

We have e⁡(X)=deg⁡(f)⋅e⁡(X)e(X)=\deg(f)\cdot e(X) and deg⁡(f)≥2\deg(f)\geq 2, so e⁡(X)=0e(X)=0. ∎

Lemma 2.14.

Any 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle over a smooth rational affine curve BB is trivial.

Proof.

The 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundles over BB are classified by He´​t1​(B,G)H^{1}_{\acute{e}t}(B,G) where G=Aut⁡(𝔸1)≅𝔾a⋊𝔾mG=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{A}^{1})\cong\mathbb{G}_{a}\rtimes\mathbb{G}_{m}. Since B⊆𝔸1B\subseteq\mathbb{A}^{1} and Pic⁡(𝔸1)=0\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbb{A}^{1})=0, we have He´​t1​(B,𝔾m)=Pic⁡(B)=0H^{1}_{\acute{e}t}(B,\mathbb{G}_{m})=\operatorname{Pic}(B)=0. Consider the short exact sequence 0→𝔾a→G→𝔾m→10\to\mathbb{G}_{a}\to G\to\mathbb{G}_{m}\to 1 and the fact that He´​t1​(B,𝔾a)=He´​t1​(B,𝔾m)=0H^{1}_{\acute{e}t}(B,\mathbb{G}_{a})=H^{1}_{\acute{e}t}(B,\mathbb{G}_{m})=0. We have He´​t1​(B,G)=0H^{1}_{\acute{e}t}(B,G)=0, which concludes the proof. ∎

Lemma 2.15.

Let KK be an algebraically closed subfield of k. Let XX be a variety over KK and f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X a dominant rational map. Then the following statements are equivalent:

(1)​K​(X)f≠K;(2)​K​(X)fℓ≠K​ for some (and hence for all) ​ℓ≥1;(3)​k​(Xk)fk≠k.(1)\;K(X)^{f}\neq K;\ (2)\;K(X)^{f^{\ell}}\neq K\text{ for some (and hence for all) }\ell\geq 1;\ (3)\;\textbf{k}(X_{\textbf{k}})^{f_{\textbf{k}}}\neq\textbf{k}.
Proof.

By [Xie19, Lemma 2.1], (1) and (2) are equivalent. The direction (1)⇒(3)(1)\Rightarrow(3) is easy. We only need to prove (3)⇒(1)(3)\Rightarrow(1). Pick ϕ∈k​(Xk)fk∖k\phi\in\textbf{k}(X_{\textbf{k}})^{f_{\textbf{k}}}\setminus\textbf{k}. View k as a KK-vector space with basis {bi}i∈I\{b_{i}\}_{i\in I}. Note that k​(Xk)≅k⊗KK⁡(X)\textbf{k}(X_{\textbf{k}})\cong\textbf{k}\otimes_{K}K(X). So we may write ϕ=∑i∈Iϕi​bi\phi=\sum_{i\in I}\phi_{i}b_{i} where ϕi∈K⁡(X)\phi_{i}\in K(X). Then ϕ=(fk)∗​ϕ=∑i∈I(f∗​ϕi)​bi\phi=(f_{\textbf{k}})^{*}\phi=\sum_{i\in I}(f^{*}\phi_{i})b_{i}, which implies f∗​ϕi=ϕif^{*}\phi_{i}=\phi_{i} for all i∈Ii\in I. Since ϕ\phi is not a constant, some ϕi\phi_{i} is nonconstant in K⁡(X)K(X) and hence K​(X)f≠KK(X)^{f}\neq K. ∎

We need the following result from [GR71, Exposé XIII, Proposition 4.6].

Lemma 2.16.

Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and XX a normal quasi-projective variety over k. Let LL be any algebraically closed field with an injective homomorphism k→L\textbf{k}\to L. Then, the natural map π1e´​t​(XL)→π1e´​t​(X)\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X_{L})\to\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X) is an isomorphism.

Lemma 2.17.

Let KK be an algebraically closed subfield of k. Let XX be a variety over KK such that XkX_{\textbf{k}} is isomorphic to a semiabelian variety (resp. an algebraic torus). Then XX is isomorphic to a semiabelian variety (resp. an algebraic torus).

Proof.

We only prove the semiabelian variety case. The algebraic torus case is similar.

By assumption, there is an isomorphism ϕk:X×Spec⁡KSpec⁡k→G\phi_{\textbf{k}}\colon X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}\textbf{k}\to G, where GG is a semiabelian variety over k (cf. 2.1). Let LL be a subfield of k such that GG (and its group structure) and ϕk\phi_{\textbf{k}} are defined over LL and LL is finitely generated over KK, i.e., there is a semiabelian variety GLG_{L} over LL and an isomorphism ϕL:X×Spec⁡KSpec⁡L→GL\phi_{L}\colon X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}\operatorname{Spec}L\to G_{L}. Then there exists an affine variety BB over KK such that K⁡(B)=LK(B)=L, a semiabelian scheme GB→BG_{B}\to B over BB whose generic fibre is GLG_{L}. After shrinking BB, there is an isomorphism of BB-schemes ϕB:X×Spec⁡KB→GB\phi_{B}\colon X\times_{\operatorname{Spec}K}B\to G_{B} whose restriction to the generic fibre is ϕL\phi_{L}. Picking b∈B⁡(K)b\in B(K), the restriction of ϕB\phi_{B} to the fibre over bb gives an isomorphism between XX and GbG_{b}. Here GbG_{b} is the fibre of GB→BG_{B}\to B over bb, which is a semiabelian variety over KK. ∎

Remark 2.18.

Let P⁡(L)P(L) be a property of algebraic varieties and morphisms over an algebraically closed field LL of characteristic zero. Assume that:

(♢\diamondsuit) for algebraically closed fields k⊆k′\textbf{k}\subseteq\textbf{k}^{\prime}, P⁡(k)P(\textbf{k}) holds true if and only if so does P⁡(k′)P(\textbf{k}^{\prime}).

Then for a fixed algebraically closed field k, P⁡(k)P(\textbf{k}) holds true if and only if so does P⁡(ℂ)P(\mathbb{C}).

Indeed, we may assume that the algebraic varieties and morphisms are defined over a subfield K⊆kK\subseteq\textbf{k} which is finitely generated over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. We then fix an embedding K⊆ℂK\subseteq\mathbb{C}. Let k1⊆ℂ\textbf{k}_{1}\subseteq\mathbb{C} (resp. k2⊆k\textbf{k}_{2}\subseteq\textbf{k}) be the algebraic closure of KK in ℂ\mathbb{C} (resp. k). Identifying the algebraic varieties and morphisms over k1\textbf{k}_{1} and k2\textbf{k}_{2} with the isomorphism induced from an isomorphism k1→k2\textbf{k}_{1}\to\textbf{k}_{2}. Then the claim follows from ( ♢ ‣ 2.18).

Lemma 2.19.

Let TT be a semiabelian variety (resp. an algebraic torus) and τ:T~→T\tau\colon\widetilde{T}\to T a finite étale cover. Then T~\widetilde{T} is also a semiabelian variety (resp. an algebraic torus).

Proof.

We may assume k=ℂ\textbf{k}=\mathbb{C} (cf. Lemmas 2.16 and 2.17 and Remark 2.18). Consider first the semiabelian variety case. Note that κ¯​(T~)=κ¯​(T)=0\overline{\kappa}(\widetilde{T})=\overline{\kappa}(T)=0. By the universal property of the quasi-Albanese map a:T~→Aa\colon\widetilde{T}\to A (cf. [Iit76]), τ\tau factors through aa. In particular, aa is a finite surjective morphism. Moreover, aa has irreducible general fibres (cf. [Kaw81, Theorem 28]). Thus aa is an isomorphism and hence XX is a semiabelian variety.

When TT is further an algebraic torus, it is affine, so is T~\widetilde{T}. Then T~\widetilde{T} being semiabelian and affine implies that it is an algebraic torus. ∎

Lemma 2.20 (cf. [NZ10, Lemma 2.12]).

Let XX be a Q-algebraic torus. Then there is a finite étale cover πT:T→X\pi_{T}\colon T\to X such that the following hold.

  1. (1)

    TT is an algebraic torus, and πT\pi_{T} is Galois.

  2. (2)

    If there is another finite étale cover πT′:T′→X\pi_{T^{\prime}}\colon T^{\prime}\to X from an algebraic torus T′T^{\prime}, then there is an étale morphism τ:T′→T\tau\colon T^{\prime}\to T such that πT′=πT∘τ\pi_{T^{\prime}}=\pi_{T}\circ\tau.

We call πT\pi_{T} the algebraic torus closure of XX.

Proof.

Since XX is a Q-algebraic torus, there is a finite étale morphism πT:T→X\pi_{T}\colon T\to X where TT is an algebraic torus. After taking its Galois closure, we may assume that πT\pi_{T} is Galois (cf. Lemma 2.19). Then X=T/GTX=T/G_{T} where GTG_{T} is a finite subgroup of Autv​a​r⁡(T)\operatorname{Aut}_{var}(T) (the automorphism group of the variety TT). Let G0=GT∩{translations on ​T}G_{0}=G_{T}\cap\{\text{translations on }T\}. Then T/G0→XT/G_{0}\to X is étale and Galois, and T/G0T/G_{0} is an algebraic torus. So we may assume GTG_{T} is translation-free. We next show that πT\pi_{T} satisfies the universal property (2).

Suppose that there is another finite étale cover πT′:T′→X\pi_{T^{\prime}}\colon T^{\prime}\to X from an algebraic torus T′T^{\prime}. By taking the base change and the Galois closure, there exist étale morphisms T~→T\widetilde{T}\to T and T~→T′\widetilde{T}\to T^{\prime} over XX such that the composition T~→X\widetilde{T}\to X is Galois. Clearly, T~\widetilde{T} is an algebraic torus (cf. Lemma 2.19). Then X≅T~/GT~X\cong\widetilde{T}/G_{\widetilde{T}} and T≅T~/HTT\cong\widetilde{T}/H_{T} where GT~G_{\widetilde{T}} is a finite subgroup of Autv​a​r⁡(T~)\operatorname{Aut}_{var}(\widetilde{T}) and HT=Gal⁡(T~/T)H_{T}=\operatorname{Gal}(\widetilde{T}/T) is a subgroup of GT~G_{\widetilde{T}}. Similarly, T′≅T~/HT′T^{\prime}\cong\widetilde{T}/H_{T^{\prime}} where HT′=Gal⁡(T~/T′)H_{T^{\prime}}=\operatorname{Gal}(\widetilde{T}/T^{\prime}) is a subgroup of GT~G_{\widetilde{T}}. Since TT and T′T^{\prime} are both algebraic tori, HTH_{T} and HT′H_{T^{\prime}} are translation subgroups of T~\widetilde{T}. By our construction of TT, the group HT=GT~∩{translations on ​T~}H_{T}=G_{\widetilde{T}}\cap\{\text{translations on }\widetilde{T}\}. So HT′H_{T^{\prime}} is a subgroup of HTH_{T}. Hence there is a natural étale morphism τ:T′→T=T′/(HT/HT′)\tau\colon T^{\prime}\to T=T^{\prime}/(H_{T}/H_{T^{\prime}}) such that πT′=πT∘τ\pi_{T^{\prime}}=\pi_{T}\circ\tau. ∎

3. Dynamical degrees and arithmetic degrees

In this section, we will upper-bound arithmetic degree by dynamical degree, and show that the arithmetic degree (like dynamical degree) is preserved by generically finite morphisms; see Propositions 3.11 and 3.13.

3.1.

The dynamical degrees. In this part, we work over an algebraically closed field of arbitrary characteristic. Let XX be a variety and f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X a dominant rational self-map. Let X′X^{\prime} be a normal projective variety which is birational to XX. Let LL be an ample (or just nef and big) divisor on X′X^{\prime}. Denote by f′f^{\prime} the rational self-map of X′X^{\prime} induced by ff. For i=0,1,…,dimXi=0,1,\dots,\dim X, and n≥0n\geq 0, define (f′n)∗​(Li)(f^{\prime n})^{*}(L^{i}) to be the (dimX−i)(\dim X-i)-cycle on X′X^{\prime} as follows: let Γ\Gamma be a normal variety with a birational morphism π1:Γ→X′\pi_{1}\colon\Gamma\to X^{\prime} and a morphism π2:Γ→X′\pi_{2}\colon\Gamma\to X^{\prime} such that f′n=π2∘π1−1f^{\prime n}=\pi_{2}\circ\pi_{1}^{-1}. Then (f′n)∗​(Li)≔(π1)∗​π2∗​(Li)(f^{\prime n})^{*}(L^{i})\coloneqq(\pi_{1})_{*}\pi_{2}^{*}(L^{i}). The definition of (f′n)∗​(Li)(f^{\prime n})^{*}(L^{i}) does not depend on the choice of Γ\Gamma, π1\pi_{1} and π2\pi_{2}. Then

di​(f)≔limn→∞((f′n)∗​(Li)⋅LdimX−i)1/nd_{i}(f)\coloneqq\lim_{n\to\infty}((f^{\prime n})^{*}(L^{i})\cdot L^{\dim X-i})^{1/n}

is called the ii-th dynamical degree of XX. The limit converges and does not depend on the choice of X′X^{\prime} and LL; moreover, if π:X⇢Y\pi\colon X\dashrightarrow Y is a generically finite and dominant rational map between varieties and g:Y⇢Yg\colon Y\dashrightarrow Y is a rational self-map such that g∘π=π∘fg\circ\pi=\pi\circ f, then di​(f)=di​(g)d_{i}(f)=d_{i}(g) for all ii; for details, we refer to [Dan20, Theorem 1] (and the projection formula), or Theorem 4 in its arXiv version.

Proposition 3.2 below is easy when k is of characteristic 00 and Z⊈Sing⁡XZ\not\subseteq\operatorname{Sing}X.

Proposition 3.2.

Let XX be a variety over an algebraically closed field k of arbitrary characteristic, and f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X a dominant rational self-map. Denote by I⁡(f)I(f) the indeterminacy locus of ff. Let ZZ be an irreducible subvariety in XX which is not contained in I⁡(f)I(f) such that f|Zf|_{Z} induces a dominant rational self-map of ZZ. Then di​(f|Z)≤di​(f)d_{i}(f|_{Z})\leq d_{i}(f) for i=0,1,…,dimZi=0,1,\dots,\dim Z.

Proof.

Set dX≔dimXd_{X}\coloneqq\dim X and dZ≔dimZd_{Z}\coloneqq\dim Z. Denote by ηZ\eta_{Z} the generic point of ZZ.

We first reduce to the projective case. Let UU be an affine open subset of XX containing ηZ\eta_{Z} and X′X^{\prime} a projective compactification of UU. Denote by f′f^{\prime} the rational self-map of X′X^{\prime} induced by ff. Note that ff is well-defined at ηZ\eta_{Z} and f⁡(ηZ)=ηZf(\eta_{Z})=\eta_{Z}. Similarly f′f^{\prime} is well-defined at ηZ\eta_{Z} and f′​(ηZ)=ηZf^{\prime}(\eta_{Z})=\eta_{Z}. Let Z′Z^{\prime} be the Zariski closure of ηZ\eta_{Z} in X′X^{\prime}. Then Z′⊈I⁡(f′)Z^{\prime}\not\subseteq I(f^{\prime}) and f′|Z′f^{\prime}|_{Z^{\prime}} induces a dominant rational self-map of Z′Z^{\prime}. After replacing X,f,ZX,f,Z by X′,f′,Z′X^{\prime},f^{\prime},Z^{\prime}, we may assume that XX is projective.

Next we reduce to the normal case. Let π:X′→X\pi\colon X^{\prime}\to X be the normalisation of XX. Set Z′≔π−1​(Z)Z^{\prime}\coloneqq\pi^{-1}(Z), the set-theoretic preimage of ZZ. It is reduced, but may not be irreducible. Let f′f^{\prime} be the rational self-map of X′X^{\prime} induced by ff. Since π\pi is finite and I⁡(f′)⊆π−1​(I⁡(f))I(f^{\prime})\subseteq\pi^{-1}(I(f)), f′f^{\prime} is well-defined at every generic point of Z′Z^{\prime}. Since f⁡(ηZ)=ηZf(\eta_{Z})=\eta_{Z} and π−1​(ηZ)\pi^{-1}(\eta_{Z}) is finite, there is some m≥1m\geq 1 and ηZ1∈π−1​(ηZ)\eta_{Z_{1}}\in\pi^{-1}(\eta_{Z}) such that (f′)m​(ηZ1)=ηZ1(f^{\prime})^{m}(\eta_{Z_{1}})=\eta_{Z_{1}}. After replacing X,f,ZX,f,Z by X′,f′m,Z1X^{\prime},f^{\prime m},Z_{1}, we may assume that XX is normal.

For n≥0n\geq 0, consider the following commutative diagram.

3.4.

Admissible triples. We define an admissible triple to be (X,f,x)(X,f,x) where XX is a quasi-projective variety over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X is a dominant rational self-map and x∈X⁡(ℚ¯)x\in X(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) such that ff is well-defined at fn​(x)f^{n}(x), for any n≥0n\geq 0.

We say that (X,f,x)(X,f,x) dominates (resp. generically finitely dominates) (Y,g,y)(Y,g,y) if there is a dominant rational map (resp. generically finite and dominant rational map) π:X⇢Y\pi\colon X\dashrightarrow Y such π∘f=g∘π\pi\circ f=g\circ\pi, π\pi is well defined along Of​(x)O_{f}(x) and π⁡(x)=y\pi(x)=y.

We say that (X,f,x)(X,f,x) is birational to (Y,g,y)(Y,g,y) if there is a birational map π:X⇢Y\pi\colon X\dashrightarrow Y such π∘f=g∘π\pi\circ f=g\circ\pi and if there is a Zariski dense open subset VV of YY containing Og​(y)O_{g}(y) such that π|U:U≔π−1​(V)→V\pi|_{U}\colon U\coloneqq\pi^{-1}(V)\to V is a well-defined isomorphism and π⁡(x)=y\pi(x)=y. In particular, if (X,f,x)(X,f,x) is birational to (Y,g,y)(Y,g,y), then (X,f,x)(X,f,x) generically finitely dominates (Y,g,y)(Y,g,y).

Remark 3.5.
  1. (1)

    If (X,f,x)(X,f,x) dominates (Y,g,y)(Y,g,y) and if Of​(x)O_{f}(x) is Zariski dense in XX, then Og​(y)O_{g}(y) is Zariski dense in YY. Moreover, if (X,f,x)(X,f,x) generically finitely dominates (Y,g,y)(Y,g,y), then Of​(x)O_{f}(x) is Zariski dense in XX if and only if Og​(y)O_{g}(y) is Zariski dense in YY.

  2. (2)

    Every admissible triple (X,f,x)(X,f,x) is birational to an admissible triple (X′,f′,x′)(X^{\prime},f^{\prime},x^{\prime}) where X′X^{\prime} is projective. Indeed, we may pick X′X^{\prime} to be any projective compactification of XX, f′f^{\prime} the self-map of X′X^{\prime} induced from ff, and x′=xx^{\prime}=x.

Lemma 3.6.

Let π:X⇢Y\pi\colon X\dashrightarrow Y be a birational map between projective varieties. Let UU be a open subset of X.X. If π\pi is well defined on UU, V≔π⁡(U)V\coloneqq\pi(U) is open in YY and π|U:U→V\pi|_{U}\colon U\to V is an isomorphism, then π−1\pi^{-1} is well defined on VV and π−1​(V)=U\pi^{-1}(V)=U.

Proof.

There are birational morphisms π1:Z→X\pi_{1}\colon Z\to X and π2:Z→Y\pi_{2}\colon Z\to Y such that π=π2∘π1−1\pi=\pi_{2}\circ\pi_{1}^{-1} and π1\pi_{1} is an isomorphism on π1−1​(U)\pi_{1}^{-1}(U). If Lemma 3.6 holds for π2\pi_{2}, then it holds for π\pi. After replacing X,π,UX,\pi,U by Z,π2,π1−1​(U)Z,\pi_{2},\pi_{1}^{-1}(U), we may assume that π\pi is a morphism.

Let U~,V~,X~,Y~\widetilde{U},\widetilde{V},\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y} be the normalisations of U,V,X,YU,V,X,Y, and π~:X~→Y~\widetilde{\pi}\colon\widetilde{X}\to\widetilde{Y} the morphism induced by π\pi. Then U~\widetilde{U} is open in X~\widetilde{X}, V~\widetilde{V} is open in Y~\widetilde{Y}, π~​(U~)=V~\widetilde{\pi}(\widetilde{U})=\widetilde{V} and π~|U~:U~→V~\widetilde{\pi}|_{\widetilde{U}}\colon\widetilde{U}\to\widetilde{V} is an isomorphism. If Lemma 3.6 holds for π~\widetilde{\pi}, then it also holds for π\pi. So we may assume that XX and YY are normal.

For every y∈Vy\in V, pick x∈Ux\in U, such that π⁡(x)=y\pi(x)=y. Then {x}=U∩π−1​(y)\{x\}=U\cap\pi^{-1}(y). So xx is an isolated point in π−1​(y)\pi^{-1}(y). By Zariski’s main theorem π−1​(y)\pi^{-1}(y) is connected. So π−1​(y)={x}\pi^{-1}(y)=\{x\}. Then π−1​(V)=U\pi^{-1}(V)=U. ∎

So we have α¯f​(x0)≤d1​(f)+r\overline{\alpha}_{f}(x_{0})\leq d_{1}(f)+r. Letting rr tend to 00, we get α¯f​(x0)≤d1​(f)\overline{\alpha}_{f}(x_{0})\leq d_{1}(f). This proves Proposition 3.11, modulo Lemma 3.12 below. ∎

Lemma 3.12.

With the assumption in the proof of Proposition 3.11, for n≥0n\geq 0, we have

hL​(fℓ​n​(x0))≤(B2​K)wn+1​C2​wn​(d1​(f)+r)ℓ⁡(n−wn)​hL​(x0).h_{L}(f^{\ell n}(x_{0}))\leq(B^{2}K)^{w_{n}+1}C^{2w_{n}}(d_{1}(f)+r)^{\ell(n-w_{n})}h_{L}(x_{0}).

Write W⁡(n)=⨆i=1m{ni,ni+1,…,ni+si−1}W(n)=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{m}\{n_{i},n_{i}+1,\dots,n_{i}+s_{i}-1\} where si≥1s_{i}\geq 1, ni+1≥ni+si+1n_{i+1}\geq n_{i}+s_{i}+1 for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m. We have ∑i=1msi=wn\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_{i}=w_{n}. In particular m≤wnm\leq w_{n}. Note that {0,…,n}∖W⁡(n)\{0,\dots,n\}\setminus W(n) is a union of at most m+1m+1 maximal subsets of consecutive numbers. Applying Inequality (8) for those maximal subsets of consecutive numbers in {0,…,n}∖W⁡(n)\{0,\dots,n\}\setminus W(n) and Inequality (9) for the others, we get

hL​(fℓ​n​(x0))\displaystyle h_{L}(f^{\ell n}(x_{0})) ≤(B2​K)m+1​C∑i=1m(si+1)​(d1​(f)+r)ℓ⁡(n−∑i=1m(si+1))​hL​(x0)\displaystyle\leq(B^{2}K)^{m+1}C^{\sum_{i=1}^{m}(s_{i}+1)}(d_{1}(f)+r)^{\ell(n-\sum_{i=1}^{m}(s_{i}+1))}h_{L}(x_{0})
=(B2​K)m+1​Cm+wn​(d1​(f)+r)ℓ⁡(n−m−wn)​hL​(x0)\displaystyle=(B^{2}K)^{m+1}C^{m+w_{n}}(d_{1}(f)+r)^{\ell(n-m-w_{n})}h_{L}(x_{0})
≤(B2​K)wn+1​C2​wn​(d1​(f)+r)ℓ⁡(n−wn)​hL​(x0).\displaystyle\leq(B^{2}K)^{w_{n}+1}C^{2w_{n}}(d_{1}(f)+r)^{\ell(n-w_{n})}h_{L}(x_{0}).

This proves Lemma 3.12 (and also Proposition 3.11). ∎

The property of KSC 1.3 is preserved under generically finite dominant morphism. Indeed:

Proposition 3.13.

Let π:X→Y\pi\colon X\to Y be a generically finite dominant morphism between quasi-projective varieties over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}. Let f:X→Xf\colon X\to X and g:Y→Yg\colon Y\to Y be quasi-finite dominant endomorphisms satisfying π∘f=g∘π\pi\circ f=g\circ\pi. Then we have:

  1. (1)

    The ff-orbit of x∈Xx\in X is Zariski dense if and only if so does the gg-orbit of π⁡(x)∈Y\pi(x)\in Y. In this case, αf​(x)\alpha_{f}(x) exists if and only if so does αg​(π​(x))\alpha_{g}(\pi(x)) and they take the same value.

  2. (2)

    KSC 1.3 holds for (X,f)(X,f) if and only if KSC 1.3 holds for (Y,g)(Y,g).

Proof.

We have d1​(f)=d1​(g)d_{1}(f)=d_{1}(g) (cf. e.g., [Dan20]). It is clear that for every x∈Xx\in X, Of​(x)O_{f}(x) is Zariski dense in XX if and only if Og​(π​(x))O_{g}(\pi(x)) is Zariski dense in YY. Note also that both π⁡(X)\pi(X) and Y∖π⁡(X)Y\setminus\pi(X) are g−1g^{-1}-invariant. Pick projective compactifications X′X^{\prime} of XX and Y′Y^{\prime} of YY such that π\pi extends to a morphism π′:X′→Y′\pi^{\prime}\colon X^{\prime}\to Y^{\prime}.

We first consider the special case where π′\pi^{\prime} is finite. Then for every ample divisor DD on Y′Y^{\prime}, π′⁣∗​D\pi^{\prime*}D is ample on X′X^{\prime}. So for every x∈Xx\in X, αf​(x)\alpha_{f}(x) and αg​(π​(x))\alpha_{g}(\pi(x)) converges in the same time and take the same value. Then KSC 1.3 holds for (X,f)(X,f) if and only if KSC 1.3 holds for (Y,g)(Y,g).

The above argument shows that we can replace X,X′,Y,Y′X,X^{\prime},Y,Y^{\prime} by their normalisations. So we may assume that all of them are normal. Let X′→π1Y1′→π2Y′X^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\pi_{1}}Y_{1}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\pi_{2}}Y^{\prime} be the Stein factorization of π′\pi^{\prime}. Set Y1≔π2−1​(Y)Y_{1}\coloneqq\pi_{2}^{-1}(Y). Since Y1Y_{1} is the normalisation of YY in k⁡(X)k(X), gg induces an endomorphism g1:Y1→Y1g_{1}\colon Y_{1}\to Y_{1} such that g1∘π1|X=π1∘fg_{1}\circ\pi_{1}|_{X}=\pi_{1}\circ f and π2∘g1=g∘π2|Y1\pi_{2}\circ g_{1}=g\circ\pi_{2}|_{Y_{1}}. Since π2\pi_{2} is finite, for every y1∈Y1y_{1}\in Y_{1}, αg1​(y1)\alpha_{g_{1}}(y_{1}) and αg​(π2​(y1))\alpha_{g}(\pi_{2}(y_{1})) converge in the same time and take the same value, and KSC 1.3 holds for (Y1,g1)(Y_{1},g_{1}) if and only if KSC 1.3 holds for (Y,g)(Y,g). After replacing Y,g,πY,g,\pi by Y1,g1,π1|XY_{1},g_{1},\pi_{1}|_{X}, we may assume that π:X→Y\pi\colon X\to Y is birational.

Let VV be the subset of YY consisting of points y∈Yy\in Y such that #​π−1​(y)=1\#\pi^{-1}(y)=1. Since Y′Y^{\prime} is normal and by applying Zariski’s Main Theorem to π′\pi^{\prime}, we have V={y∈Y∣dimπ−1​(y)=0}V=\{y\in Y\mid\dim\pi^{-1}(y)=0\}. Moreover, π|U:U≔π−1​(V)→V\pi|_{U}\colon U\coloneqq\pi^{-1}(V)\to V is an isomorphism. Since gg is quasi-finite, both VV and Y∖VY\setminus V are g−1g^{-1}-invariant. In particular, for x∈Xx\in X (resp. y∈Yy\in Y), if Of​(x)O_{f}(x) (resp. Og​(y)O_{g}(y)) is Zariski dense, we have Of​(x)⊆UO_{f}(x)\subseteq U (resp. Og​(y)⊆VO_{g}(y)\subseteq V). Then (X,f,x)(X,f,x) is birational to (Y,g,π⁡(x))(Y,g,\pi(x)). Now Proposition 3.13 follows from Lemma 3.8. ∎

Lemma 3.14 below allows us to replace ff by any positive power whenever needed.

Lemma 3.14.

Let XX be a (quasi-projective, when we discuss KSC 1.3) variety and f:X⇢Xf\colon X\dashrightarrow X a dominant rational self-map. The following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    (X,f)(X,f) satisfies ZDO 1.1 (resp. AZO 1.2, KSC 1.3).

  2. (2)

    There is an ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, such that (X,fℓ)(X,f^{\ell}) satisfies ZDO 1.1 (resp. AZO 1.2, KSC 1.3).

Proof.

For the ZDO and AZO parts, we refer to [Xie19, Propositions 2.2 and 3.27].

For the KSC part, note that d1​(f)ℓ=d1​(fℓ)d_{1}(f)^{\ell}=d_{1}(f^{\ell}) and αf​(x)ℓ=αfℓ​(x)\alpha_{f}(x)^{\ell}=\alpha_{f^{\ell}}(x) when the latter exists, for any ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 and x∈Xx\in X (cf. 3.9 (iii)). Also, Of​(x)O_{f}(x) is Zariski dense if and only if so is Ofℓ​(x)O_{f^{\ell}}(x). Then the lemma follows. ∎

4. Endomorphisms descending along a fibration

This section treats endomorphisms descending along fibrations, especially 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibrations.

Lemma 4.1.

Let XiX_{i}, BiB_{i} be varieties, and πi:Xi→Bi\pi_{i}\colon X_{i}\to B_{i} a surjective morphism with a general fibre irreducible (i=1,2i=1,2). Let f:X1→X2f\colon X_{1}\to X_{2} be a finite surjective morphism which descends to a surjective morphism g:B1→B2g\colon B_{1}\to B_{2}. Then f|(X1)b:(X1)b→(X2)g⁡(b)f|_{(X_{1})_{b}}\colon(X_{1})_{b}\to(X_{2})_{g(b)} is surjective for any closed point b∈B1b\in B_{1}.

Proof.

Set X2′≔X2×B2B1X_{2}^{\prime}\coloneqq X_{2}\times_{B_{2}}B_{1}. Since a general fibre of π2\pi_{2} is geometrically irreducible, X2′X_{2}^{\prime} is irreducible. Denote by ϕ1:X2′→X2\phi_{1}\colon X_{2}^{\prime}\to X_{2} and ϕ2:X2′→B1\phi_{2}\colon X_{2}^{\prime}\to B_{1} the two natural projections, respectively. The natural morphism τ:X1→X1×B2B1\tau\colon X_{1}\to X_{1}\times_{B_{2}}B_{1} is a closed embedding, noting that gg is separated. Since ff is finite, f×B2id:X1×B2B1→X2′=X2×B2B1f\times_{B_{2}}\operatorname{id}\colon X_{1}\times_{B_{2}}B_{1}\to X_{2}^{\prime}=X_{2}\times_{B_{2}}B_{1} is finite. Then f′≔(f×B2id)∘τ:X1→X2′f^{\prime}\coloneqq(f\times_{B_{2}}\operatorname{id})\circ\tau\colon X_{1}\to X_{2}^{\prime} is finite. We have the following commutative diagram.

Since ϕ1\phi_{1} is generically finite and ff is surjective, f′f^{\prime} is dominant. Then f′f^{\prime} being finite and dominant implies it is surjective. For any b∈B1b\in B_{1}, f′​((X1)b)=(X2′)bf^{\prime}((X_{1})_{b})=(X_{2}^{\prime})_{b}. Since ϕ1​((X2′)b)=(X2)g⁡(b)\phi_{1}((X_{2}^{\prime})_{b})=(X_{2})_{g(b)}, we have f⁡((X1)b)=ϕ1​(f′​((X1)b))=ϕ1​((X2′)b)=(X2)g⁡(b)f((X_{1})_{b})=\phi_{1}(f^{\prime}((X_{1})_{b}))=\phi_{1}((X_{2}^{\prime})_{b})=(X_{2})_{g(b)}. ∎

Lemma 4.2.

Let f:X1→X2f\colon X_{1}\to X_{2} be a morphism between normal varieties, and πi:Xi→Bi\pi_{i}\colon X_{i}\to B_{i} a surjective morphism to a smooth curve (i=1,2i=1,2). Suppose that a general fibre F1F_{1} of π1\pi_{1} is irreducible. Suppose further that f⁡(F1)f(F_{1}) is contained in a fibre of π2\pi_{2} (this holds when F1F_{1} is a curve with κ¯​(B2)>κ¯​(F1)\overline{\kappa}(B_{2})>\overline{\kappa}(F_{1}), e.g., when π1\pi_{1} is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration and κ¯​(B2)≥0\overline{\kappa}(B_{2})\geq 0). Then ff descends to a morphism f|B1:B1→B2f|_{B_{1}}\colon B_{1}\to B_{2} (which is surjective if so is ff).

Proof.

Take normal compactifications Xi⊆Xi¯X_{i}\subseteq\overline{X_{i}}, Bi⊆Bi¯B_{i}\subseteq\overline{B_{i}} such that the natural extensions πi¯:Xi¯⇢Bi¯\overline{\pi_{i}}\colon\overline{X_{i}}\dashrightarrow\overline{B_{i}} (i=1,2i=1,2) and f¯:X1¯⇢X2¯\overline{f}\colon\overline{X_{1}}\dashrightarrow\overline{X_{2}} are morphisms.

Since B1¯\overline{B_{1}} is smooth of dimension one, π1¯\overline{\pi_{1}} is flat and hence has equi-dimensional connected fibres. By the assumption and the rigidity lemma, π2¯∘f¯\overline{\pi_{2}}\circ\overline{f} contracts one and hence every fibre of π1¯\overline{\pi_{1}}, and then π2¯∘f¯\overline{\pi_{2}}\circ\overline{f} factors through π1¯\overline{\pi_{1}} via some f¯|B1¯:B1¯→B2¯\overline{f}|_{\overline{B_{1}}}\colon\overline{B_{1}}\to\overline{B_{2}}. Since π1:X1→B1\pi_{1}\colon X_{1}\to B_{1} is surjective, every b∈B1b\in B_{1} is mapped to π2​(f⁡((X1)b))∈B2\pi_{2}(f((X_{1})_{b}))\in B_{2}, i.e., f¯|B1¯​(B1)⊆B2\overline{f}|_{\overline{B_{1}}}(B_{1})\subseteq B_{2}. Hence the (surjective) morphism f:X1→X2f\colon X_{1}\to X_{2} descends, via the surjections πi:Xi→Bi\pi_{i}\colon X_{i}\to B_{i}, to a (surjective) morphism f|B1:B1→B2f|_{B_{1}}\colon B_{1}\to B_{2}.

Note that if F1F_{1} is a curve and f⁡(F1)f(F_{1}) dominates B2B_{2} via π2\pi_{2} then κ¯​(F1)≥κ¯​(f⁡(F1))≥κ¯​(B2)\overline{\kappa}(F_{1})\geq\overline{\kappa}(f(F_{1}))\geq\overline{\kappa}(B_{2}), and note also κ¯​(𝔸1)=−∞\overline{\kappa}(\mathbb{A}^{1})=-\infty. Then the lemma follows. ∎

Proposition 4.3.

Let π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B be a surjective morphism from a normal quasi-projective variety to a smooth curve with a general fibre irreducible. Let f:X→Xf\colon X\to X be a finite surjective morphism which descends to a surjective morphism g:B→Bg\colon B\to B (this is the case when Lemma 4.2 is satisfied). Let Σ0⊆B\Sigma_{0}\subseteq B (resp. Σ1⊆B\Sigma_{1}\subseteq B) be the set of b∈Bb\in B such that the fibre XbX_{b} is reducible (resp. irreducible and non-reduced). Then we have:

  1. (1)

    g−1​(Σ0)=Σ0g^{-1}(\Sigma_{0})=\Sigma_{0}. Hence gg induces a surjective endomorphism of B∖Σ0B\setminus\Sigma_{0}.

  2. (2)

    If gg is étale (this is the case when κ¯​(B)≥0\overline{\kappa}(B)\geq 0; cf. Lemma 2.12), then g−1​(Σ1)=Σ1g^{-1}(\Sigma_{1})=\Sigma_{1}, hence gg induces a surjective endomorphism of B∖(Σ0∪Σ1)B\setminus(\Sigma_{0}\cup\Sigma_{1}).

  3. (3)

    If κ¯​(B)=1\overline{\kappa}(B)=1, or if κ¯​(B)≥0\overline{\kappa}(B)\geq 0 and π\pi has a reducible fibre or a non-reduced fibre, then gg is an automorphism of finite order.

Proof.

Lemma 4.1 implies that ff maps the fibre XbX_{b} onto Xg⁡(b)X_{g(b)} for any b∈Bb\in B. Thus g−1​(Σ0)⊆Σ0g^{-1}(\Sigma_{0})\subseteq\Sigma_{0}. Now Σ0\Sigma_{0} is a finite set, so g−1​(Σ0)=Σ0g^{-1}(\Sigma_{0})=\Sigma_{0}.

If gg is étale, then g∗​bg^{*}b is reduced for any b∈Bb\in B. This implies that g−1​(Σ1)⊆Σ1g^{-1}(\Sigma_{1})\subseteq\Sigma_{1}. Since Σ1\Sigma_{1} is a finite set, we have g−1​(Σ1)=Σ1g^{-1}(\Sigma_{1})=\Sigma_{1}.

(3) follows from (1), (2) and Lemma 2.11. ∎

Lemma 4.4.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface and π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration. Then every fibre has support equal to a disjoint union of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}’s. Hence, either π\pi is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle, or it has a reducible or non-reduced fibre.

Proof.

Extend π\pi to π¯:X¯→B¯\overline{\pi}\colon\overline{X}\to\overline{B} from a smooth projective surface to a smooth projective curve with the boundary D=X¯∖XD=\overline{X}\setminus X an SNC divisor. Then DD consists of a cross-section of π\pi and some fibre components. Noting that DD supports a connected ample effective divisor by Lemma 2.2, the affine XX contains no compact ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, and every fibre of π¯:X¯→B¯\overline{\pi}\colon\overline{X}\to\overline{B} consists of ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}’s and has dual graph a connected tree, the lemma follows. ∎

Proposition 4.5.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface over k and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a finite surjective morphism. Let π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B be a surjective 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration. Suppose that |π1e´​t​(X)|=∞|\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X)|=\infty, and B=𝔸1B=\mathbb{A}^{1} or ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. Then ff descends to an automorphism f|Bf|_{B} on BB of finite order.

Proof.

Our proof closely follows [GZ08, Lemmas 3.5–3.6]. We consider the case B=𝔸1B=\mathbb{A}^{1} only since the case B=ℙ1B=\mathbb{P}^{1} is similar.

We first prove that the surjective endomorphism ff descends to a surjective endomorphism f|Bf|_{B} on BB. By Lemma 4.2, we only need to show the property P⁡(k)P(\textbf{k}): f⁡(F)f(F) is contained in a fibre of π\pi for a general fibre FF of π\pi. The property P⁡(k)P(\textbf{k}) satisfies ( ♢ ‣ 2.18) of Remark 2.18. So we may assume k=ℂ\textbf{k}=\mathbb{C}. Note that the (topological) fundamental group π1​(X)\pi_{1}(X) of XX is infinite by the assumption that |π1e´​t​(X)|=∞|\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{\acute{e}t}}(X)|=\infty.

Let F1,…,FrF_{1},\dots,F_{r} be all multiple fibres of π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B with multiplicity mi≥2m_{i}\geq 2 (cf. Definition 2.8). If r≤1r\leq 1, then π1​(X)\pi_{1}(X) is finite cyclic of order upper-bounded by the multiplicity of FrF_{r} (cf. Proof of [Nor83, Lemma 1.5], or [GMM20, Lemma 1.1.11]). Thus r≥2r\geq 2.

By Proposition 2.9, there is a finite surjective morphism B′→BB^{\prime}\to B with ramification index equal to mim_{i} at every point of B′B^{\prime} lying over the point π⁡(Fi)\pi(F_{i}) such that the normalisation X′X^{\prime} of X×BB′X\times_{B}B^{\prime} is étale over XX, the induced fibration π′:X′→B′\pi^{\prime}\colon X^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} has no multiple fibre and the fibres of π′\pi^{\prime} lying over FiF_{i} are all reducible (see also Lemma 4.4).

Suppose the contrary that the property P⁡(ℂ)P(\mathbb{C}) is false. Then the normalisation of f⁡(F)f(F) equals 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} (because κ¯​(f⁡(F))≤κ¯​(F)=κ¯​(𝔸1)=−∞\overline{\kappa}(f(F))\leq\overline{\kappa}(F)=\overline{\kappa}(\mathbb{A}^{1})=-\infty), so it is simply connected and dominates BB via π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B. Take an irreducible component F′⊆X′F^{\prime}\subseteq X^{\prime} of the inverse of f⁡(F)f(F) via the étale map X′→XX^{\prime}\to X. Then F′F^{\prime} has normalisation equal to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1} and dominates B′B^{\prime}. Thus −∞=κ¯​(𝔸1)≥κ¯​(π′​(F′))≥κ¯​(B′)-\infty=\overline{\kappa}(\mathbb{A}^{1})\geq\overline{\kappa}(\pi^{\prime}(F^{\prime}))\geq\overline{\kappa}(B^{\prime}). So B′≅𝔸1B^{\prime}\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}. This and that π′:X′→B′\pi^{\prime}\colon X^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} has all fibres non-multiple, with the help of [Nor83, Lemma 1.5], imply that π1​(X′)=(1)\pi_{1}(X^{\prime})=(1). Hence π1​(X)\pi_{1}(X) is finite too, a contradiction to the assumption. Thus P⁡(ℂ)P(\mathbb{C}) and hence P⁡(k)P(\textbf{k}) hold true. So ff descends to a surjective endomorphism f|Bf|_{B}.

Next we show that f|Bf|_{B} is an automorphism of finite order. Clearly, this property also satisfies ( ♢ ‣ 2.18) of Remark 2.18. So we may assume that k=ℂ\textbf{k}=\mathbb{C} in the following.

Let Σ0⊆X\Sigma_{0}\subseteq X (resp. Σ0′⊆X′\Sigma_{0}^{\prime}\subseteq X^{\prime}) be the set of points over which the fibres of π\pi (resp. π′\pi^{\prime}) are reducible. By Proposition 4.3, (f|B)−1​(Σ0)=Σ0(f|_{B})^{-1}(\Sigma_{0})=\Sigma_{0}. Iterating ff, we may assume that f−1f^{-1} stabilises every component in every reducible fibre of π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B. Thus f|Bf|_{B} restricts to a surjective endomorphism of B∖Σ0B\setminus\Sigma_{0}.

The argument in [GZ08, Lemma 3.5] shows that ff induces an isomorphism of the group π1​(X)\pi_{1}(X). Thus the covering theory implies that ff lifts to a finite surjective morphism f′:X′→X′f^{\prime}\colon X^{\prime}\to X^{\prime}, via the étale covering X′→XX^{\prime}\to X.

By the compatibility of f,πf,\pi on XX and f′,π′f^{\prime},\pi^{\prime} on X′X^{\prime}, our f′f^{\prime} descends to a surjective morphism f′|B′:B′→B′f^{\prime}|_{B^{\prime}}\colon B^{\prime}\to B^{\prime}. The same Proposition 4.3 implies that (f′|B′)−1​(Σ0′)=Σ0′(f^{\prime}|_{B^{\prime}})^{-1}(\Sigma_{0}^{\prime})=\Sigma_{0}^{\prime} and f′|B′f^{\prime}|_{B^{\prime}} restricts to a surjective endomorphism of B′∖Σ0′B^{\prime}\setminus\Sigma_{0}^{\prime}.

Note that |Σ0′|≥2|\Sigma_{0}^{\prime}|\geq 2 (since the fibres lying over the r≥2r\geq 2 of fibres FiF_{i} are reducible). Thus B′∖Σ0′B^{\prime}\setminus\Sigma_{0}^{\prime} is the affine curve B′B^{\prime} with at least two points removed, hence κ¯​(B′∖Σ0′)=1\overline{\kappa}(B^{\prime}\setminus\Sigma_{0}^{\prime})=1 (alternatively, since all fibres of the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration π′:X′→B′\pi^{\prime}\colon X^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} are non-multiple, |π1​(X′)|=∞|\pi_{1}(X^{\prime})|=\infty and [Nor83, Lemma 1.5] imply that |π1​(B′)|=∞|\pi_{1}(B^{\prime})|=\infty, so κ¯​(B′)≥0\overline{\kappa}(B^{\prime})\geq 0). Therefore, f′|B′∖Σ0′f^{\prime}|_{B^{\prime}\setminus\Sigma_{0}^{\prime}} and hence f|Bf|_{B} are automorphisms of finite order (cf. Lemma 2.11). ∎

Lemma 4.6.

Let πi:Xi→Bi\pi_{i}\colon X_{i}\to B_{i} be an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle from a smooth surface to a smooth curve (i=1,2i=1,2). Let f:X1→X2f\colon X_{1}\to X_{2} be a finite surjective morphism which descends to a surjective morphism g:B1→B2g\colon B_{1}\to B_{2}. Take any ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-bundle πi′:Vi→Bi\pi_{i}^{\prime}\colon V_{i}\to B_{i} as a partial compactification of πi\pi_{i} (which exists by Lemma 2.3). Then ff extends to a surjective morphism f:V1→V2f\colon V_{1}\to V_{2}.

Proof.

Note that Hi=Vi∖XiH_{i}=V_{i}\setminus X_{i} is an irreducible πi′\pi_{i}^{\prime}-horizontal curve since every fibre of πi:Xi→Bi\pi_{i}\colon X_{i}\to B_{i} is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}. Extend ff as a rational map f:V1⇢V2f:V_{1}\dasharrow V_{2} with indeterminacy being several points on H1H_{1}. Take a composition of blow ups μ:V1′→V1\mu\colon V_{1}^{\prime}\to V_{1} such that f′=f∘μf^{\prime}=f\circ\mu is a morphism and μ⁡(Exc⁡(μ))⊆H1\mu(\operatorname{Exc}(\mu))\subseteq H_{1}. Since ff descends to gg, we have π2∘f′=g∘π1∘μ\pi_{2}\circ f^{\prime}=g\circ\pi_{1}\circ\mu. Take a (−1)(-1)-curve C⊆Exc⁡(μ)C\subseteq\operatorname{Exc}(\mu). If f′​(C)f^{\prime}(C) is not a point, then f′​(C)=H2f^{\prime}(C)=H_{2}, since f−1​(X2)=X1f^{-1}(X_{2})=X_{1}; but then π2​(f′​(C))=g⁡(π1​(μ⁡(C)))\pi_{2}(f^{\prime}(C))=g(\pi_{1}(\mu(C))) is a point, a contradiction. Lemma 4.7.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a finite surjective morphism with deg⁡(f)≥2\deg(f)\geq 2. Let π:X→B\pi\colon X\to B be a surjective 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-fibration. 6. Case of log Kodaira dimension ≥0\geq 0: Proofs of Theorems 1.7 and 1.8

This section deals with smooth affine surfaces of non-negative log Kodaira dimensions.

Proposition 6.1.

By the log ramification divisor formula, KΓ+DΓ=pi∗​(KV+D)+EiK_{\Gamma}+D_{\Gamma}=p_{i}^{*}(K_{V}+D)+E_{i} for some effective divisor EiE_{i} for i=1,2i=1,2 (cf. [Iit82, Theorem 11.5]). Now the following composition self-map f∗f^{*} is an injective linear transformation

and hence an isomorphism, for any s≥1s\geq 1.

Take ss sufficiently large and divisible. Then Φ|s⁡(KV+D)|=Φ|s​P|\Phi_{|s(K_{V}+D)|}=\Phi_{|sP|} as rational maps, where the latter is a well-defined morphism (the Iitaka fibration of XX) with connected fibres. Proposition 6.2.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface over k, and f:X→Xf\colon X\to X a finite surjective morphism of degree ≥2\geq 2. Suppose κ¯​(X)=0\overline{\kappa}(X)=0. When dimS=1\dim S=1 (resp. dimA=1\dim A=1) we set Y≔SY\coloneqq S (resp. Y≔AY\coloneqq A); when S=TS=T and dimT=2\dim T=2, we let T→Y≔𝔾mT\to Y\coloneqq\mathbb{G}_{m} be any projection; let b:X→Yb:X\to Y be the natural dominant morphism, and FF its general fibre. By Iitaka’s subadditivity (cf. [Iit82, Theorem 11.15]), 0=κ¯​(X)≥κ¯​(F)+κ¯​(b⁡(X))≥κ¯​(F)+κ¯​(Y)0=\overline{\kappa}(X)\geq\overline{\kappa}(F)+\overline{\kappa}(b(X))\geq\overline{\kappa}(F)+\overline{\kappa}(Y). By the easy addition (cf. [Iit82, Theorem 11.9]), 0=κ¯​(X)≤κ¯​(F)+dimY0=\overline{\kappa}(X)\leq\overline{\kappa}(F)+\dim Y; hence κ¯​(F)≠−∞\overline{\kappa}(F)\neq-\infty. Combining the above all, we get κ¯​(F)=0=κ¯​(Y)\overline{\kappa}(F)=0=\overline{\kappa}(Y) and bb is surjective. Hence F≅𝔾mF\cong\mathbb{G}_{m} since F⊆XF\subseteq X is affine, and either YY is an elliptic curve or Y≅𝔾mY\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}. Thus X→YX\to Y is a surjective 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-fibration. Since e⁡(X)=0e(X)=0 by Lemma 2.13, every fibre of π\pi has support 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} by the Suzuki formula (cf. [Suz77], [Gur97]).

By Proposition 2.9, there is a finite surjective morphism ϕ:B′→B\phi\colon B^{\prime}\to B such that the normalisation X′X^{\prime} (still affine) of X×BB′X\times_{B}B^{\prime} is étale over XX and the induced morphism π′:X′→B′\pi^{\prime}\colon X^{\prime}\to B^{\prime} is a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle. By Lemma 2.6, κ¯​(B′)=κ¯​(X′)\overline{\kappa}(B^{\prime})=\overline{\kappa}(X^{\prime}) (=κ¯​(X)=0=\overline{\kappa}(X)=0). This and Corollary 2.7 imply that B′≅𝔾mB^{\prime}\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}. By Lemma 2.6 again, there is a finite étale cover θ:B′′→B′\theta:B^{\prime\prime}\to B^{\prime} (of degree ≤2\leq 2) such that the base change π′′:X′′→B′′\pi^{\prime\prime}\colon X^{\prime\prime}\to B^{\prime\prime} of π′\pi^{\prime} via θ\theta is a trivial 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle. Since B′B^{\prime} is isomorphic to 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m} so is its étale cover B′′B^{\prime\prime}. Now X′′X^{\prime\prime} is a trivial 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle over B′′≅𝔾mB^{\prime\prime}\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}, so X′′≅𝔾m2X^{\prime\prime}\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}. This proves Claim 6.3. ∎

We return back to the proof of Proposition 6.2. Now for a general field k, we can use the same argument as in Remark 2.18 to conclude that XX is a Q-algebraic torus over k, with the help with Claim 6.3 and Lemma 2.17; note that any (connected) finite étale cover of XkX_{\textbf{k}} comes from a such one of XℂX_{\mathbb{C}} (cf. Lemma 2.16). Then, as a consequence of Lemma 2.20, ff lifts to the algebraic torus closure πT:T≅𝔾m2→X\pi_{T}\colon T\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\to X. ∎

Now we are ready for the following two proofs.

Proof of Theorem 1.7.

It follows from Propositions 6.1 (and its proof) and 6.2. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.8.

By Remark 1.4, for the ZDO 1.1 part, we only need to prove AZO 1.2; further, for the AZO 1.2 part, we may assume that (X,f)(X,f) is defined over an algebraically closed field whose transcendence degree over ℚ\mathbb{Q} is finite. For the KSC 1.3 part, as usual, we assume that (X,f)(X,f) is defined over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}. By [Xie19, Corollary 3.31], we may assume that deg⁡(f)≥2\deg(f)\geq 2.

If κ¯​(X)=2\overline{\kappa}(X)=2, then ff is an automorphism of finite order by Lemma 2.11, contradicting the extra assumption that deg⁡(f)≥2\deg(f)\geq 2.

If κ¯​(X)=1\overline{\kappa}(X)=1, then Proposition 6.1 implies that there is a finite étale cover ϕ:X′′→X\phi\colon X^{\prime\prime}\to X such that X′′X^{\prime\prime} admits a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle structure π′′:X′′→B′′\pi^{\prime\prime}\colon X^{\prime\prime}\to B^{\prime\prime} and some iteration of ff lifts to f′′:X′′→X′′f^{\prime\prime}\colon X^{\prime\prime}\to X^{\prime\prime} and satisfies π′′∘f′′=π′′\pi^{\prime\prime}\circ f^{\prime\prime}=\pi^{\prime\prime}. Thus AZO 1.2 and KSC 1.3 hold for (X′′,f′′)(X^{\prime\prime},f^{\prime\prime}) and hence also for (X,f)(X,f) (cf. Lemma 3.14, [Xie19, Lemma 3.28] and Proposition 3.13).

If κ¯​(X)=0\overline{\kappa}(X)=0, then by Proposition 6.2, there is a finite étale cover ϕ:𝔾m2→X\phi\colon\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\to X such that ff lifts to f′:𝔾m2→𝔾m2f^{\prime}\colon\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\to\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}. AZO 1.2 for semiabelian varieties is proved in Theorem 1.5 and KSC 1.3 for them is proved in [MS20]. So AZO 1.2 and KSC 1.3 hold for (X,f)(X,f) too (cf. [Xie19, Lemma 3.28] and Proposition 3.13). ∎

7. Extensions of polynomial maps: Proofs of Theorems 1.9 and 1.11

The aim of this section is to show that Adelic Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture (AZO 1.2) is stable under extension by polynomial maps (cf. Theorem 7.1). With the help of this, we prove Theorems 1.9 and 1.11.

Let k be an algebraically closed field of finite transcendence degree over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. We prove:

Theorem 7.1.

Let XX be a projective variety over k, and f1:X⇢Xf_{1}\colon X\dashrightarrow X a dominant rational self-map. Assume that AZO 1.2 holds for the pair (X,f1)(X,f_{1}) (this is the case when dimX=1\dim X=1, cf. Lemma 3.14). Let f2∈k​(X)​[y]∖k​(X)f_{2}\in\textbf{k}(X)[y]\setminus\textbf{k}(X) be a nonconstant polynomial. Then AZO 1.2 and hence ZDO 1.1 hold for the dominant rational self-map f:X×ℙ1⇢X×ℙ1f\colon X\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\dashrightarrow X\times\mathbb{P}^{1} sending (x,y)(x,y) to (f1​(x),f2​(x,y))(f_{1}(x),f_{2}(x,y)).

Definition 7.2.

We say a pair (X,f)(X,f) satisfies Strong Adelic Zariski Dense Orbit-property (SAZO-property for short) if the ff-orbit of an adelic general point is well-defined and Zariski dense in XX.

Proof of Theorem 7.1.

The proof is similar to the proof of [Xie19, Theorem 4.1]. In this proof, we follow the notation in [Xie19, Section 3.1]. We may replace f1f_{1} and ff by iterations (cf. Lemmas 2.15 and 3.14).

If H∈k​(X)f1∖kH\in\textbf{k}(X)^{f_{1}}\setminus\textbf{k}, then π∗​H∈k​(X×ℙ1)f∖k\pi^{*}H\in\textbf{k}(X\times\mathbb{P}^{1})^{f}\setminus\textbf{k}. So we may assume that SAZO-property holds for (X,f1)(X,f_{1}). For every z∈X×ℙ1z\in X\times\mathbb{P}^{1} (resp. x∈Xx\in X), denote by Zf​(z)Z_{f}(z) (resp. Zf1​(x)Z_{f_{1}}(x)) the Zariski closure of the ff-orbit Of​(z)O_{f}(z) of zz (resp. the f1f_{1}-orbit Of1​(x1)O_{f_{1}}(x_{1}) of xx).

If degy⁡(f2)=1\deg_{y}(f_{2})=1, Theorem 7.1 holds by [Xie19, Theorem 3.32]. Now assume d≔degy⁡(f2)≥2d\coloneqq\deg_{y}(f_{2})\geq 2. Write f2​(x,y)=∑i=0dai​(x)​yif_{2}(x,y)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{i}(x)y^{i} with ai∈k​(X)a_{i}\in\textbf{k}(X). There is a Zariski dense open subset X′X^{\prime} of XX such that ai∈𝒪⁡(X′)a_{i}\in\mathcal{O}(X^{\prime}) (0≤i≤d0\leq i\leq d) and ad​(x)≠0a_{d}(x)\neq 0 for any x∈X′x\in X^{\prime}.

We may assume that there is a nonempty adelic open subset A⊆XA\subseteq X such that for every x∈Ax\in A, the f1f_{1}-orbit of xx is well-defined and Zariski dense in XX. Let KK be a subfield of k which is finitely generated over ℚ\mathbb{Q}, such that K¯=k\overline{K}=\textbf{k} and f1,f2,Xf_{1},f_{2},X are defined over KK.

By [Xie19, Proposition 3.22], replacing ff by an iteration, there is a nonempty adelic open subset B⊆(X×ℙ1)​(k)B\subseteq(X\times\mathbb{P}^{1})(\textbf{k}) such that for every point z∈Bz\in B, the ff-orbit of zz is well-defined and Zf​(z)Z_{f}(z) is irreducible. By [Xie19, Proposition 3.22] again, replacing ff by a positive power, we may assume that there exist a prime p≥3p\geq 3, an embedding i:K↪ℂpi\colon K\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}_{p}, and an open subset V≃(ℂp∘)dimXV\simeq(\mathbb{C}_{p}^{\circ})^{\dim X} of XK​(ℂp)X_{K}(\mathbb{C}_{p}) which is f1f_{1}-invariant, such that the f1f_{1}-orbits of the points in VV are well-defined and f1|V=idmodpf_{1}|_{V}=\operatorname{id}\,\bmod\;p. In particular, f1pn​(x)→xf_{1}^{p^{n}}(x)\to x when n→∞n\to\infty for every x∈Vx\in V.

There is some M≥1M\geq 1 such that for every i=0,1,…,di=0,1,\dots,d and x∈Vx\in V, we have |ai​(x)|≤M|a_{i}(x)|\leq M and |ad​(x)|≥M−1|a_{d}(x)|\geq M^{-1}. Pick some R>M2R>M^{2}.     the orbits of zz and π⁡(z)\pi(z) are well-defined;

  3. (3)

    Zf​(z)Z_{f}(z) is irreducible;

  4. (4)

    Zf1​(π⁡(z))×{∞}⊆Zf​(z)Z_{f_{1}}(\pi(z))\times\{\infty\}\subseteq Z_{f}(z); and
